title-group.article-title: Baseline Cognitive and Neurological Status Does Not Modify the Occurrence of ICANS in CAR T‐Cell Therapy for Aggressive B‐Cell Lymphoma

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) is a common, serious complication of CAR T‐cell therapy for blood cancers. This study evaluates the impact of baseline cognitive status and pre‐existing neurological injury on the occurrence of ICANS.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We conducted a prospective study of adult patients treated with CAR T‐cell therapy for aggressive B‐cell lymphoma at our centre between May 2020 and December 2023. All patients underwent neurological examination, cerebral MRI and cognitive assessment measured by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). We measured total metabolic tumour volume (TMTV), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), albumin, ferritin and C‐reactive protein (CRP) before CART cell infusion, and serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels. We evaluated the impact of these factors on ICANS occurrence using multivariate analysis.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Among the 156 adult patients treated with CAR T‐cell therapy, 32.7% developed ICANS. The median MoCA score at baseline was 26 [IQR 24; 28]. There was no significant association between the onset of ICANS and baseline cognitive performance (p 0.57). MoCA scores did not differ by ICANS grade. Pre‐existing neurological injury were not associated with increased ICANS risk. In multivariable analysis, the use of CD28 CAR T cells was the strongest predictor of ICANS (p = 0.007). Slightly elevated serum NfL levels at leukapheresis predicted ICANS (p = 0.046) supporting its role in predicting risk of neurotoxicity rather than pre‐existing neurological disease.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our results suggest that pre‐existing cognitive impairment or neurological history do not increase the risk of ICANS.

abstract.p: ICANS risk after CAR T‐cell therapy is independent of baseline neurological or cognitive status.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T‐cell therapy has dramatically modified the landscape of cancer treatment, particularly in haematological malignancies [1, 2]. Although its efficacy in inducing durable remissions is undeniable, the occurrence of neurotoxicity is a major challenge as it induces acute morbidity, potentially requiring ICU transfer and prolonged hospitalisation [3, 4].

Neurotoxicity associated with CAR T‐cell therapy manifests as cognitive and, to a lesser extent, non‐pyramidal motor disorders. Cognitive dysfunction occurs in almost all patients, with 36% experiencing severe symptoms and is a hallmark of immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS). These cognitive symptoms encompass a wide range of issues, including aphasia, agraphia, executive dysfunction, cognitive slowing, apraxia, disorientation, agitation, dyscalculia, hemineglect syndrome, hallucinations and confusional states, which can appear independently or in combination [5, 6].

Predicting which patients will develop neurotoxicity, as well as the timing and severity of symptoms, remains a challenge. Unlike cytokine release syndrome (CRS), neurotoxicity is only partially responsive to treatment and often requires prolonged hospitalisation and supportive care. Previous studies have identified a number of potential predictive factors for neurotoxicity in order to establish preventive management, early intervention and avoid prolonged hospitalisation. The most established risk factors for ICANS are similar to those for CRS: high disease burden [7, 8], CAR T‐cell construct [9, 10, 11] and in vivo CAR T‐cell expansion [7, 10, 12]. Higher pretreatment ferritin, CRP and pre‐existing neurological comorbidity [13, 14], including baseline brain MRI abnormalities [14, 15], have also been suggested to predict ICANS. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) can help monitor neurological toxicity during CAR T‐cell therapy in paediatric patients [16]. Moreover, serum NfL levels prior to CAR T‐cell infusion may correlate with the severity of ICANS [17, 18, 19]. We therefore decided to include NfL as a biomarker in the multivariate analysis.

The objective of this prospective study is to investigate the influence of cognitive status, measured by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) test, and pre‐existing neurological conditions on the incidence and severity of ICANS. A secondary multivariate analysis will examine the relationships between cognitive status, pre‐existing neurological lesions and established and proposed risk factors to better understand their contributions to the occurrence of ICANS.

sec.title: Study Design and Participants
sec.p: This prospective observational study included all adult patients with aggressive B‐cell lymphoma treated with CAR T‐cell therapy at our specialised lymphoma referral centre between May 2020 and December 2023. We excluded patients who were unable to read and write in French, those with central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma, patients undergoing second‐round CAR T‐cell therapy, and those who had received a lymphodepleting regimen with bendamustine. This study was approved by the local institutional review board for ethics and clinical research ‘Comité Local d'Ethique pour la Recherche Clinique des HUPSSD Avicenne‐ Jean Verdier‐René Muret’ (CLEA‐2019‐74) and was conducted in accordance with the STROBE statement [20]. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: A senior neurologist conducted a thorough neurological examination, an assessment of pre‐existing neurological conditions, a brain MRI, and a global cognitive assessment using the MoCA test within 2 weeks prior to CAR T‐cell infusion. We selected the MoCA test because it is a validated and widely used tool, valued for its ability to provide a rapid and comprehensive assessment of global cognitive function, making it particularly suitable for use in clinical practice. Pre‐existing neurological injury or disease was defined based on a documented neurological history and/or abnormal findings on baseline brain MRI. We defined abnormal brain MRI as the presence of vascular‐origin changes such as moderate to severe leukopathy (Fazekas 2 and 3), chronic post‐stroke lesions, or chronic subdural hematoma. Neurological comorbidities were systematically assessed through a structured questionnaire administered to all patients by the clinical team. The presence of any prior neurological history was documented by the treating clinician, with standardized questions to gather information about past brain injuries, neurological disorders and stroke history. Acute neurotoxicity was managed according to our institution's standard of care [6, 21] and monitored by a neurologist. CRS and ICANS were graded according to the ASCT consensus criteria [22]. The neurology committee, composed of expert neurologists (RU, SC, CB, MES, CB and AC), systematically reviewed all neurological symptoms documented in clinical notes and discharge summaries, from CAR T‐cell infusion up to 6 months and ICANS grades. We retrospectively recorded total metabolic tumor volume (TMTV), biological data including lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), before CAR T‐cell infusion at the time of lymphodepletion. Baseline laboratory values, including C‐reactive protein (CRP), albumin and ferritin, were measured on the day of CAR T‐cell infusion. Patients received axicabtagene‐ciloleucel (axi‐cel), brexucabtagene autoleucel (brexu‐cel), tisagenlecleucel (tisa‐cel) or lisocabtagene maraleucel (liso‐cel), depending on slot availability and underlying disease. All patients received lymphodepleting chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide and fludarabine. Prophylactic corticosteroids and/or tocilizumab were not used.

sec.title: NfL Quantification
sec.p: The NfL was included as a biological risk factor. Patient's serum samples were collected on the day of leukapheresis and stored at the Immunology Laboratory at −80°C. NfL levels were quantified using the Ella automated simple plex immunoassay system (lower limit of quantification 1.09 pg/mL) (Bio‐Techne).

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Standard descriptive statistics were used to summarise baseline demographic, clinical and biological characteristics. Categorical variables are presented as numbers and percentages, while quantitative variables are expressed as medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs). Patients with ICANS (grades 1–4) were compared to those without ICANS. Group comparisons were performed using Pearson's chi‐squared test with Yates' continuity correction or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables, and the Welch Two Sample t‐test or Wilcoxon rank‐sum test with continuity correction for quantitative variables, as appropriate. Effect sizes were reported following the guidelines of Funder (2019) and Cohen (1988). Odds ratios (ORs) associated with ICANS occurrence were computed using logistic regression models. All variables significantly associated with ICANS in the univariate analysis were included in the multivariate analysis. A logistic regression model (estimated using maximum likelihood) was fitted to predict ICANS. Missing data were not imputed. Standardised parameters were obtained by fitting the model to a standardised version of the dataset. 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and p‐values were calculated using a Wald z‐distribution approximation. All tests were two‐tailed with α = 0.05. All statistical analyses were performed using ‘R++, l'essentiel’ for Windows, Version 1.7.04, Toulouse, France.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: We identified 213 adult patients who received CAR T‐cell therapy for aggressive B‐cell lymphoma between May 2020 and December 2023 (Figure 1).

Of these, 156 patients were included in the study, with a median age of 64.5 years (IQR 56–70.3) and 55 females and 101 males. A total of 92 (58.97%) patients received CD28‐containing CAR T‐cells (82 axi‐cel, 10 brexu‐cel) and 64 (41.03%) received 4‐1BB‐containing CAR T‐cells (60 tisa‐cel, 4 liso‐cel) (Table 1).

Overall, 52 (32.69%) patients developed ICANS, with 19 (12.2%) experiencing grade 1, 17 (10.9%) grade 2, 7 (4.5%) grade 3 and 8 (5.1%) grade 4 neurotoxicity. The distribution of patient characteristics according to ICANS grade is summarized in the Table 1. The median onset of ICANS was 6 days (IQR 4.5–10), and its median duration was 8 days (IQR 4–18). Cognitive dysfunction was the most common sign of neurotoxicity.
We initially performed a univariate analysis to assess the correlation of each parameter with the occurrence of ICANS, comparing patients who developed ICANS with those who did not.

In univariate analysis, we examined various parameters, including total metabolic tumour volume (TMTV), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), C‐reactive protein (CRP), albumin, and ferritin levels prior to CAR T‐cell infusion (Table 2). Only the use of CD28‐based CAR T‐cells (p = 0.007) and elevated baseline CRP (p = 0.02) were significantly associated with the occurrence of ICANS (Tables 1 and 2).

caption.p: Patients biomarkers on the day of leukapheresis and CAR T‐cell infusion.

fn.p: Note: Bold values are statistically significant.

sec.p: The administration of CD28‐constructed CAR T‐cells was also associated with the occurrence of a higher grade of ICANS p = 0.007 (Table S1).

The median baseline MoCA score was 26 (IQR 24–28) (Table 2), and although baseline cognitive performance was not significantly correlated with ICANS occurrence (p = 0.57; 95% CI [−1.34, 0.74]), the distribution of MoCA scores did not vary according to ICANS grade: the median MoCA score was 26 for ICANS grades 1, 2, and 4 and 28 for grade 3 ICANS (Figure 2).

caption.p: Distribution of baseline MoCA scores by ICANS grade.

sec.p: We decided to quantify NfL levels in serum samples collected at the time of leukapheresis, which would be a good time to decide whether or not to proceed with CAR T‐cell production. Median serum NfL levels were 54.6 pg/mL [IQR 31.8–86.2]. In univariate analyses, baseline serum NfL levels were not significantly associated with the occurrence of ICANS of any grade (p = 0.11) (Table 2). The distribution of serum NfL levels at the leukapheresis time point and occurrence of ICANS is shown in Figure 3.

caption.p: Distribution of serum NfL levels at the leukapheresis and occurrence of ICANS.

sec.p: To evaluate risk factors for the occurrence of any grade of neurotoxicity in the multivariate analyses based on the parameters described above, we first fitted a logistic model to predict ICANS using the following parameters: CD28 vs. 4‐1BB co‐stimulatory domain, TMTV level and abnormal LDH and CRP level. Within this model, only the effect of CD28 vs. 4‐1BB was statistically significant and positive (p = 0.009; 95% CI [0.29, 1.88]) (Table 3).

caption.p: Multivariate logistic model to predict ICANS with patient's biomarkers.

fn.p: Note: Bold values are statistically significant.

sec.p: Next, we aimed to determine whether other factors describing pre‐existing neurological conditions could predict ICANS. The distribution of pre‐existing neurological conditions is summarised in Table S2. To address this, we performed a multivariate analysis by constructing a logistic regression model. The CAR construct with a CD28 domain, the strongest predictor of ICANS occurrence (compared to the 4‐1BB CAR T construct), was included alongside the variables of interest: serum NfL levels at leukapheresis (pg/mL), baseline MoCA score, abnormal brain MRI and previous neurological history. In this model, both NfL levels at leukapheresis and CD28 co‐stimulatory domain (compared to 4‐1BB) were statistically significant positive predictors of ICANS (p = 0.046, OR 1.01, 95% CI [1.00011, 1.01159] and p = 0.007, OR 3.18, 95% CI [1.37, 7.39], respectively) (Table 4). The effect of these parameters on low (0–1) and high [2, 3, 4] grade ICANS was similar (p = 0.025, OR 1.01, 95% CI [1.0009, 1.01322] and p = 0.003, OR 5.86, 95% CI [1.83, 18.75], respectively) (Table S3).

caption.p: Multivariate logistic model to predict ICANS.

fn.p: Note: Bold values are statistically significant.

sec.p: We also aimed to investigate these parameters in the group of 63 patients with a pathological MoCA score below 26 [23]. Among them, 19 (30%) developed ICANS. We examined whether MoCA scores varied by ICANS grade and whether CAR T constructs, serum NfL levels, MRI results and previous neurological history could predict the occurrence of high‐grade ICANS. However, neither univariate nor multivariate analyses (Table S4) identified any of these factors as being associated with ICANS severity.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Neurotoxicity associated with CAR T‐cell therapy occurs in approximately one third of patients. Despite progress in understanding the underlying mechanisms, predicting neurotoxicity remains a challenge. Current efforts are focused on identifying biomarkers and establishing risk scores based on clinical and laboratory parameters to improve the prediction of toxicity associated with CAR T‐cell therapies.

In B‐ALL patients, pre‐existing neurological conditions have been linked to increased CAR T‐cell–related neurotoxicity: Gofshteyn et al. reported an association with prior neurological deficits, although no detailed sub‐analysis was provided [13]; Gust et al. found links with MRI abnormalities [14] and comorbidities such as seizures or prior CNS toxicity [24], baseline imaging was not performed in all patients [14], limiting generalizability; Leahy et al. identified CNS relapse as the only significant risk factor [15].

However, this has not been formally demonstrated, as pivotal clinical trials excluded patients with secondary CNS lesions and neurological comorbidities due to concerns about neurotoxicity. As a result, the direct impact of pre‐existing cognitive dysfunction on ICANS risk remains an open question. In our study, we sought to investigate the impact of neurological factors as potential predictors of ICANS, as well as biological markers previously identified in the literature. The biomarkers were selected based on previous studies that identified them as significant ICANS risk factors, highlighting the role of systemic inflammation and immune activation in neurotoxicity. This single‐centre cohort study was conducted at our specialised lymphoma referral centre, where we analysed 156 adult patients treated with CAR T‐cell therapy. Of these, 32.7% developed ICANS, with high‐grade (grade 3–4) events occurring in 9.6% and no grade 5 events reported. This is in line with reported ICANS rates, which typically range from 37.5% to 77% depending on the CAR T‐cell product used and the study population [9, 25].

The median onset of ICANS in our study was 6 days of infusion, which is consistent with data showing that most cases of ICANS occur within 8 days of infusion [5, 26]. In our study, the median baseline MoCA score was 26 (IQR [24; 28]). The presence of ICANS was not significantly associated with baseline cognitive performance, with a p‐value of 0.57 and a 95% CI of [−1.34, 0.74] (Figure 2). In addition, there was no increased risk of neurotoxicity in patients with pre‐existing neurological conditions such as baseline cognitive deficits, abnormal brain MRI, or previous neurological history in univariate and multivariate analysis. Patients with low MoCA scores (< 26) had the same ICANS incidence (30%), regardless of abnormal brain MRI or prior neurological history. This suggests that baseline cognitive impairment, as assessed by MoCA, may not be a major determinant of ICANS susceptibility. Other factors, such as inflammatory mechanisms or individual neuroplasticity, could play a more critical role and warrant further investigation. Therefore, our data showed no significant association between pre‐existing neurological conditions and ICANS risk, contrary to the hypothesis raised by other authors [13, 14, 27]. One possible explanation for our findings is the complexity of the mechanisms underlying ICANS. While ICANS is indeed a neurological dysfunction driven by immune responses and cytokine release, it is possible that previous neurological injury (as indicated by poor MOCA scores) does not predispose patients to developing ICANS [28]. While pre‐existing neurological conditions may intuitively appear to increase risk, the immune and systemic responses leading to neurotoxicity may override any pre‐existing vulnerabilities, making other factors such as treatment type, immune system activity and general health more important in determining the occurrence of ICANS [28, 29, 30, 31]. In line with previous studies, we found that CD28‐based CAR T‐cell therapies were significantly associated with a higher risk of ICANS (p = 0.007). In fact, Gust et al. [14] showed that CD28 co‐stimulatory domains were associated with earlier and more severe neurotoxicity compared to 4‐1BB domains. This is likely due to faster proliferation and cytokine release driven by CD28 signalling [12, 32, 33] contributing to the inflammatory cascade that triggers ICANS [14]. On the other hand, 4‐1BB CAR T cells tend to induce a more gradual and sustained T‐cell expansion, reducing the likelihood of acute neurotoxicity [32]. This difference between CD28‐ and 4‐1BB‐based constructs is consistently reported across studies [9, 10, 11, 25]. Neither high serum LDH prior to lymphodepleting chemotherapy nor large TMTV on PET‐TDM prior to CAR T‐cell infusion was associated with ICANS. This may be due to our selection of patients with limited TMTV for CAR T‐cell therapy and adaptation of the bridging therapy without bendamustine as well.

In a wide range of neurological disorders, neurofilament proteins have emerged as critical biomarkers of neuroaxonal injury, with applications in the preclinical diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases, as well as markers of disease progression, prognosis and therapeutic response [34, 35]. Although NfL levels are not disease‐specific, their diagnostic and prognostic value is well established in various contexts.

In our study, serum NfL levels measured on the day of leukapheresis were identified as significant predictors of ICANS (p = 0.046). This finding aligns with our earlier report linking elevated serum NfL levels at leukapheresis or prior to CAR T‐cell infusion with the occurrence of grades 2 to 4 ICANS [19]. Notably, this study expands on prior work by including patients with pre‐existing cognitive impairments or neurological conditions, which were excluded in the earlier analysis. These results underscore the robustness of NfL as a predictor of ICANS across diverse patient populations [16, 17].

Additionally, the association between NfL and ICANS across all grades, with no significant differences between them, highlights its potential as an early biomarker for neurotoxicity in CAR T‐cell therapy. These findings contribute to the growing evidence supporting the role of NfL in predicting ICANS and emphasize the need for continued research to refine its application in clinical practice, especially across diverse patient populations.

One of the key strengths of our study is the larger cohort size compared to previous investigations focusing on cognitive function and pre‐existing neurological conditions [24, 36, 37, 38]. This comprehensive analysis of all patients represents a broader dataset than those previously reported [17, 18]. However, several limitations warrant discussion. The MoCA test may overlook subtle cognitive vulnerabilities predisposing patients to ICANS, affecting baseline interpretations. Future studies should consider incorporating more detailed neuropsychological assessments to capture nuanced cognitive deficits. Additionally, NfL levels were not corrected for confounding factors such as age, BMI, or kidney function, which may influence results [34, 39]. Future research should account for these variables to refine the assessment of the relationship between NfL levels and ICANS risk. Another limitation is the inability to calculate the m‐EASIX (Endothelial Activation and Stress Index) score [40, 41] due to missing parameters like platelet count. This prevented us from evaluating its prognostic value. Recent studies suggest that factors such as low platelet count, female sex, and specific therapeutic regimens may predict severe ICANS [42]. Including platelet count in future registries would enable more robust analyses. Finally, we excluded patients with CNS lymphoma (n = 12) due to significant pre‐existing cognitive impairments that rendered the MoCA test unsuitable. However, prior research indicates that including these patients does not necessarily increase ICANS incidence [26, 43]. Future studies should explore alternative cognitive assessment tools to evaluate this subgroup and validate whether findings on ICANS risk factors are applicable to broader populations, including those with severe neurological comorbidities.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In conclusion, our results suggest that pre‐existing cognitive status or neurological injury does not increase the risk of ICANS. In contrast, the use of a CD28 co‐stimulatory domain and elevated baseline inflammatory markers such as CRP were significantly associated with ICANS. Serum NfL levels at leukapheresis emerged as a promising early biomarker of neurotoxicity. These findings support the potential of NfL as a valuable risk stratification tool and potentially improve patient monitoring and guide early intervention strategies in CAR T‐cell therapy. Our study suggests that immune‐mediated neuroinflammation, rather than pre‐existing neurological vulnerability, may be involved in the development of ICANS. These findings highlight the need for personalised risk stratification and further research into the mechanisms linking immune activation to neurotoxicity. However, further studies are needed to refine predictive models and explore additional risk factors to improve patient outcomes.
